chapters.title: Chapter 1: How Income Tax in India Is Structured

lessons.title: From Gross Income to Taxable Income: Where the Slabs Come In

body.text: Slabs never touch your CTC. They are applied to what is left after exempt income is removed, each head of income is computed and eligible deductions are subtracted. Every rupee removed before that point is a rupee the slabs never see.

children.text: An offer letter from TCS or Flipkart says ₹15 lakh CTC. Your bank account sees salary credits, FD interest and perhaps a dividend from ITC. None of these numbers is what the slab table is applied to. Between the money you earn and the slab calculation sits a short, fixed sequence of steps, and knowing it tells you exactly where tax can and cannot be reduced.
The Five-Step Journey to Taxable Income
Remove exempt income.
Some receipts are not income for tax purposes at all, such as PPF interest and maturity, or a gift from your parents. They leave the calculation here and never come back.
Classify and compute income under each head.
Every taxable rupee is placed under one of five heads. Each head has its own rules and its own allowances, such as the standard deduction from salary.
Set off losses.
Permitted losses, such as a business loss, are adjusted against income. The rules on which losses can be set off against which head are strict.

markDefs.definition: The total of income under all five heads, after setting off permitted losses but before subtracting deductions such as employer NPS contributions or, under the old regime, Section 80C.

children.text: Arrive at
Gross Total Income
, then subtract deductions.
Deductions for investments and payments, such as an employer's NPS contribution, come off Gross Total Income. The old regime allows many more of these than the new regime.
Round off to get Total Income.
The result is rounded to the nearest multiple of ₹10. This Total Income, also called taxable income, is what the slabs are applied to.

body.latex: \text{Total Income} = \underbrace{\sum_{\text{5 heads}} \text{Income under each head} - \text{Losses set off}}_{\text{Gross Total Income}} - \text{Deductions}
body.caption: Exempt income never enters this equation

children.text: The Five Heads of Income

body.caption: Where Each Type of Income Goes

cells: Pay and taxable perks from an employer, including pension
Monthly salary from Wipro, a bonus, employer NPS contribution
Standard deduction of ₹75,000 (new regime) or ₹50,000 (old regime)
Rent from buildings or land attached to them that you own
Rent from a 2BHK let out in Noida
30% of the annual value as a flat deduction for repairs
Profits and Gains of Business or Profession
Income from a business, trade, freelancing or professional practice
Fees earned by a freelance UX designer; F&O trading on NSE
Profit on selling a capital asset
Selling Reliance shares on Zerodha, selling a plot in Nashik
Taxable income that fits no other head
Savings account and FD interest, dividends, taxable gifts

children.text: The standard deduction for salaried employees sits in section 19 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (section 16(ia) of the Income-tax Act, 1961). It needs no proof and no investment. If you receive a salary or pension, you get it automatically, which is why it survives in both regimes.

body.text: Capital gains are part of Gross Total Income, but most of them are not taxed through the slabs. Equity gains, for example, carry their own special rates. For now, treat "income taxed at slab rates" as salary, house property, business and other sources. Chapter 4 shows how special-rate income is taxed alongside slab income.

body.title: Pick the Right Head
body.question: Ravi, a salaried employee in Kochi, earns ₹42,000 of interest on a fixed deposit with Federal Bank. Under which head is this taxed?
options: Salaries, because Ravi is a salaried employee
Capital Gains, because the FD is an investment
It is exempt, because bank interest is already subject to TDS
body.explanation: Interest from FDs and savings accounts is taxed under Income from Other Sources, at slab rates. TDS is only an advance collection of tax. It does not make the interest exempt, and the interest must still be added to your income.

children.text: What the New Regime Still Lets You Deduct

body.title: Deductions Before the Slabs: New Regime vs Old Regime

columns.label: New Regime (Default)
points: Standard deduction of ₹75,000 from salary or pension
Employer's contribution to your NPS account, up to 14% of basic salary plus DA
30% deduction and interest on a let-out property's home loan, against its rent
Deduction for family pension, up to ₹25,000
No Section 80C, 80D, HRA exemption or self-occupied home loan interest

columns.label: Old Regime (Opt-In)
points: Standard deduction of ₹50,000 from salary or pension
Employer NPS contribution, up to 10% of basic salary plus DA
Section 80C investments such as EPF, PPF and ELSS, up to ₹1,50,000
Section 80D health insurance, HRA and LTA exemptions
Interest on a self-occupied home loan, up to ₹2,00,000

body.text: This course focuses on how slabs work, so we will not go deeper into individual deductions here. For the complete list of what each regime allows and how to decide between them, see our course Old Tax Regime vs New Tax Regime: Which One to Choose.

children.text: Worked Example: Sneha's Journey From ₹16 Lakh to Taxable Income

Sneha is a data engineer in Pune on the new regime for tax year 2026-27. Her basic salary is ₹6,00,000. Her gross salary, including a ₹70,000 employer NPS contribution, is ₹15,50,000. She also earns ₹12,000 of savings account interest, ₹38,000 of FD interest and ₹21,000 of interest credited to her PPF account.

body.caption: Sneha's Computation of Taxable Income, New Regime

cells: Employer NPS contribution (within 14% of basic, i.e. ₹84,000)

body.title: Sneha's ₹16,00,000 of Taxable Receipts: How Much Reaches the Slabs

data.label: Total Income taxed at slab rates

children.text: Only now do the slabs come in. On ₹14,55,000: the first ₹4,00,000 is nil, the next ₹4,00,000 at 5% is ₹20,000, the next ₹4,00,000 at 10% is ₹40,000, and the remaining ₹2,55,000 at 15% is ₹38,250. Her slab tax is ₹98,250. The rebate test, surcharge and cess all come after this, and Chapter 3 picks up the calculation from exactly here.

stats.label: Total Income
stats.context: What the slabs are applied to

children.text: Why a Deduction Is Worth Less Than Its Face Value

Because deductions come off income before the slabs are applied, a deduction removes income from your highest slab first. Sneha's ₹70,000 employer NPS deduction came entirely out of her 15% slab. It saved her ₹10,500 of slab tax, plus ₹420 of cess, not ₹70,000. The value of any deduction is roughly the deduction multiplied by your top slab rate. Chapter 2 explores this idea properly.

body.label: Tax Saved by a Deduction
body.value: Deduction × your top slab rate (plus cess)
body.context: Holds as long as the deduction does not push income down into a lower slab. If it does, each slice saves tax at the rate of the slab it came from.

children.text: Practice

body.title: Arjun's Taxable Income
body.prompt: Arjun, a bank officer in Indore, is on the new regime for tax year 2026-27. His gross salary is ₹11,00,000 and his employer makes no NPS contribution. He earns ₹45,000 of FD interest and ₹18,000 of PPF interest, and receives a gift of ₹2,00,000 from his father. What is his Total Income for the slab calculation?
body.explanation: Salary ₹11,00,000 less the ₹75,000 standard deduction gives ₹10,25,000. Add FD interest of ₹45,000 under Other Sources: ₹10,70,000. PPF interest is exempt, and a gift from a parent is exempt because parents count as relatives, so neither enters. There are no new regime deductions to claim, so Total Income is ₹10,70,000.

body.title: Name the Stage
body.textWithBlank: The total of income under all five heads, after setting off permitted losses but before deductions, is called ___.
body.explanation: Gross Total Income is the stage between the heads of income and deductions. Subtracting eligible deductions from it gives Total Income, the figure the slabs are applied to.

body.title: The ₹50,000 That Is Not Worth ₹50,000
body.scenario: Karan, a consultant in Delhi on the new regime, has Total Income of ₹18,00,000. HR offers to restructure his pay so that ₹50,000 goes into NPS as an employer contribution, well within the 14% of basic limit. A friend tells him: "Take it. That's ₹50,000 less tax."
body.prompt: How much tax does the restructuring actually save Karan, including 4% cess?
body.modelAnswer: The deduction reduces Karan's Total Income from ₹18,00,000 to ₹17,50,000. The whole ₹50,000 comes out of his 20% slab (16 to 20 lakh), so slab tax falls by ₹10,000. Cess of 4% on that is ₹400, so the total saving is ₹10,400, not ₹50,000. Whether it is worth doing also depends on whether he is comfortable with the money being locked into NPS until retirement.

points: Slabs are applied to Total Income, never to CTC, gross salary or bank credits
The sequence is: remove exempt income, compute income under five heads, set off losses, subtract deductions, round to the nearest ₹10
The five heads are Salaries, House Property, Business or Profession, Capital Gains and Other Sources
The new regime still allows the ₹75,000 standard deduction and the employer NPS deduction, among a few others
Most capital gains are part of Gross Total Income but are taxed at special rates, not slab rates
A deduction saves tax at roughly your top slab rate, not rupee for rupee

body.text: Figures in this lesson apply to resident individuals for tax year 2026-27 under the Income-tax Act, 2025. Deduction limits and eligibility can change in each Union Budget. This lesson is for education only and is not tax advice.
